final.summary: Recommended: llm:direct. Peak 90th pct core temp 37.71 °C (limit 38.0), tightest margin 0.28 °C, 5% of priority-weighted work done.
reasons: **Heat safety is protected, but just barely.** Under this plan, even the hardest-working crew members are expected to stay below the body heat limit (about 37.7 °C against a limit of 38.0 °C). The closest call leaves only about a quarter of a degree of breathing room, so anything that adds heat, like a hotter day, heavier gear, or skipped breaks, could push someone over.

**Very little of the important work gets done.** Keeping everyone that cool means only about 5% of the high-priority work gets finished. Expect most of the job to be pushed to later shifts or cooler conditions.

**The other option we tested was worse.** A plan designed to get more work done ended up finishing none of the priority work and ran just as hot. So this schedule is the better of the two, but the real limit is the heat, not the planning. Getting more done would likely take changes on the ground, such as more shade, more water, cooling gear, extra crew, or working cooler hours.

Hard safety rules:
- Every worker's 90th percentile core temperature must stay below 38.0 °C all shift. Harder work, sun and high WBGT heat people up; 30-min shade rests cool them down.
- Breaks: at most 3 work slots in a row, then a 'rest' slot; at most 2 in a row if any of those slots has WBGT >= 30.0 °C.
- No outdoor tasks during hazards that stop outdoor work. After lightning, outdoor work stays stopped for 30 more minutes.
- Workers who are not acclimatized never do very_heavy tasks when WBGT >= 28.0 °C.
Validity: one entry per slot per worker; off-site workers rest; skills and allowed slots must match.
